blk_part_02_part_2_turkus_history_church.text: Turku's story begins with the church. In 1229, a letter from Pope Gregory IX moved the seat of the local bishop to the area around Turku. Many people count this as the start of the city. The bishop's great church, Turku Cathedral, was probably consecrated on 17 June 1300. "Consecrated" means it was officially made a holy place. In Swedish, the city is called Åbo, and both names are still used.

blk_part_02_part_2_turkus_history_church.text: In 1827 the Great Fire of Turku began on 4 September and destroyed about 75 percent of the city. The Great Fire of Turku left 11,000 people homeless, and 27 deaths were recorded. The fire damaged Turku Cathedral and the main building of the Imperial Academy of Turku, also called the Royal Academy of Turku, which had been founded in 1640. After the fire, the Academy moved to Helsinki. Today it is the University of Helsinki. The architect Carl Ludvig Engel then drew a new plan for Turku with wider streets.

His Finlandia Hall, a concert and congress hall by Töölö Bay, was finished in 1971. It is covered in white Carrara marble and black granite. It was meant to balance Engel's Senate Square and to celebrate Finnish independence. In 1975, it hosted a famous international meeting that led to the Helsinki Accords. In 2012, Helsinki was named World Design Capital.
